section_summary: Pages 1–31 are a continuation of the file’s chronological “List of Papers,” indexing 1938 diplomatic reports, congressional correspondence, public protests, petitions, and Department replies about exports of arms, scrap iron, oil, aircraft, and other strategic materials to Japan. Pages 32–62 contain the opening substantive correspondence: citizens and labor or church groups urge an embargo, while the State Department repeatedly explains that the Neutrality Act cannot prohibit scrap-iron or other raw-material exports and has not been invoked against either belligerent. The section also includes a naval attaché report on Japanese scrap purchases in Nicaragua, a union protest concerning a government-owned ship, reports of the Nanking atrocities, and petitions from Seattle churches.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Army Equipment—Japan, entries 171–452
subfiles.about: A chronological index summarizes diplomatic reports, citizen protests, petitions, congressional referrals, and replies concerning military and strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This continuation of the file index begins with entry 171 and records documents from early 1938 through November. Most entries concern demands that the United States stop exporting arms, airplanes, scrap iron, petroleum, cotton, trucks, and other materials useful to Japan's war in China. Department replies typically transmitted the Neutrality Act or related pamphlets and explained the absence of legal authority for a unilateral embargo. The index also identifies diplomatic reporting on Japanese procurement in Europe, Asia, and the Americas.

subfiles.title: Ludella W. Goodspeed protest against oil and iron exports
subfiles.about: Goodspeed asks the President to prevent oil and iron from being exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The badly fragmented page preserves a Seattle address, White House referral markings, and portions of Goodspeed's request concerning oil and iron exports. The file index identifies it as a protest urging that such exports to Japan be discontinued.

subfiles.title: Reply to Ludella W. Goodspeed
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department states that no existing statute authorizes the President to prohibit oil and iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Goodspeed's undated letter, which had been referred by the White House. He gives a brief legal answer: current statutes do not empower the President to prohibit the exportation of oil and iron to Japan.

subfiles.title: C. A. Hayes letter and clipping on Japanese pig-iron purchases
subfiles.about: Hayes forwards a newspaper report alleging that Japan was buying American pig iron and industrial equipment for naval armament.
subfiles.summary: The surviving cover page is poorly legible, but the file index identifies Hayes's letter as a protest concerning pig-iron exports to Japan. The enclosed Associated Press clipping quotes Upton Close, also identified as Josef Washington Hall, predicting conflict with Japan and asserting that Japanese battleship materials came from Birmingham and Pittsburgh. It also reports his expectation that Japan would seize iron deposits near Hankow on the Yangtze River.

subfiles.title: Reply to C. A. Hayes
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department advises Hayes that the President lacks statutory power to prohibit pig-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost acknowledges Hayes's February 19 letter and its newspaper clipping. He states that no existing statute authorizes the President to prohibit exports of pig iron to Japan.

subfiles.title: Los Angeles County District Council of Carpenters request for an embargo
subfiles.from: C. R. Van Winkle, Los Angeles County District Council of Carpenters
subfiles.about: The carpenters' council asks Roosevelt to support an embargo on war and potential war materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Van Winkle writes under instructions from the Los Angeles County District Council of Carpenters. He argues that peaceful pressure, especially denial of war materials, could halt Japanese aggression in China. The letter presents an embargo as a means of advancing both world peace and American security.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to C. R. Van Winkle
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why most raw-material exports could not legally be stopped.
subfiles.summary: Yost transmits the Joint Resolution and presidential proclamation of May 1, 1937. He explains that a presidential finding of a state of war would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, but that no legal authority permits discrimination against Japan alone. Apart from narrow statutory exceptions such as tin-plate scrap and helium, other materials could not be prohibited. Roosevelt had concluded that invoking the resolution in the Far Eastern conflict would not serve the country's broader interests.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on Japanese purchases of Nicaraguan scrap iron
subfiles.to: Office of Naval Intelligence, Navy Department
subfiles.about: The report summarizes Nicaraguan press claims that local scrap iron was being bought for shipment to Japan and conversion into armaments.
subfiles.summary: The attaché reports that La Nueva Prensa said J. Antonio Tijerino sold the old ship Momotombo to Morris Pataky, who intended to resell it as scrap to a Japanese firm. La Noticia further alleged that Pataky's represented company was buying all available iron for export to Japan. The attaché adds that, while in Panama, he heard that the Panama Canal Department had sold substantial scrap to Japanese buyers and that USS Charleston moved so a Japanese vessel could load it.

subfiles.title: National Maritime Union telegram protesting scrap-iron transport
subfiles.from: Fredrick Myers, National Maritime Union Committee
subfiles.about: Myers protests the use of a government-owned merchant ship to carry 5,000 tons of scrap iron from Brooklyn to Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: The telegram identifies the City of Rayville as loading scrap iron at Brooklyn's Pier 16 for Yokohama. Myers argues that transporting material widely understood to be used for war violates the spirit of the Nine-Power Treaty, the Kellogg–Briand Pact, and the State Department's restrictions on war cargoes. He asks Hull to intervene with the Commerce Department and stop the loading.

subfiles.title: Reply to Fredrick Myers on scrap iron aboard government-owned vessels
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains that scrap iron is not legally classified as an implement of war and may therefore be exported on government-owned merchant vessels.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Myers's protest and encloses the President's September 14, 1937 statement, the arms-traffic pamphlet, and the Joint Resolution. He explains that scrap iron is absent from the categories of arms, ammunition, and implements of war enumerated in the relevant proclamations and conventions. Consequently, no restriction applies to its export to Japan, regardless of whether a government-owned merchant vessel carries it.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Henry B. Twombly's letter
subfiles.about: Roosevelt asks the Secretary of State to reply to Henry B. Twombly's enclosed letter.
subfiles.summary: The brief White House memorandum refers Twombly's communication to the Secretary of State. Roosevelt asks that a reply be prepared and sent.

subfiles.title: Henry B. Twombly letter on the Nanking atrocities and American exports
subfiles.about: After hearing George Fitch's eyewitness account of Nanking, Twombly asks the President to stop American war materials from reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Twombly recounts a luncheon with George Fitch, recently returned from China after participating in relief work during the siege of Nanking. Fitch's account leads Twombly to compare the Japanese atrocities unfavorably even with Tilly's sack of Magdeburg. Twombly argues that supplying Japan contradicts American sympathy for China and asks Roosevelt to find a means of stopping the flow of war material.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Henry B. Twombly
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department explains the decision not to invoke the Neutrality Act and supplies comparative arms-export licensing figures for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green states that without a presidential finding of a state of war there is no authority to prohibit arms exports either to both belligerents or to Japan alone. He says Roosevelt considered invocation of the Joint Resolution contrary to the practical interests of the United States and its nationals. Since July 1, 1937, the Department had licensed $12,136,114.16 in arms exports to China and $5,907,658.28 to Japan.

subfiles.title: Henry B. Twombly acknowledgment
subfiles.about: Twombly thanks Green for the reply and notes approvingly that licensed arms exports to China exceeded those to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Twombly acknowledges Green's letter and the enclosed Joint Resolution. He expresses satisfaction that a larger proportion of exported armament was going to China, while condemning Japan's manner of warfare there.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on rayon-contaminated cotton waste
subfiles.about: The memorandum calls attention to a Kobe report that legally required rayon admixture made Japanese cotton-cloth waste unsuitable for ammunition manufacture.
subfiles.summary: The writer describes Kobe despatch no. 238 as an amusing sidelight on Japanese mobilization. Because domestic “cotton” textiles contained legally mandated rayon, their waste reportedly performed poorly as material for ammunition production. The memorandum recommends reading the brief report.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hong Kong despatch on the Lin Ma Hang Lead Mine
subfiles.about: The sheet redirects researchers to a despatch about Japanese lead purchases and operation of the Lin Ma Hang Lead Mine.
subfiles.summary: This document-file note records Hong Kong despatch no. 136 of March 16, 1938. It cross-references the purchase of lead in Hong Kong by Japan and encloses or points to a memorandum on the Lin Ma Hang Lead Mine under another decimal-file number.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner cover letter to the President
subfiles.about: Hiltner tells Roosevelt that he is sending Hull petitions from Seattle citizens protesting scrap-iron and war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner reports sending the Secretary of State a packet bearing several hundred signatures and encloses a copy of his covering letter. He closes with a religious expression of support for Roosevelt during national and international crises.

subfiles.title: Walter G. Hiltner letter transmitting Seattle church petitions
subfiles.about: Hiltner forwards church petitions and describes Seattle opposition to a recent scrap-iron shipment to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hiltner says the signatures were collected quickly from Seattle church members and ministers, with additional lists expected. He describes a recent ship heavily laden with scrap iron for Japan and a silent picket by prominent local citizens. Labor, church, and business organizations, he says, broadly resent the continued export of scrap and other war materials, which the petitions ask the government to stop.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Walter G. Hiltner
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the petitions and explains why neither scrap-iron exports nor arms exports to Japan alone could be prohibited under existing law.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Hiltner for the petitions and encloses the May 1, 1937 Joint Resolution and the pamphlet International Traffic in Arms. He explains that invoking neutrality would prohibit covered arms exports to both China and Japan, while scrap iron was not among the legally enumerated implements of war. No statute therefore authorized the President to prohibit scrap-iron exports to any foreign country. Roosevelt had also concluded that invoking the resolution in the Far Eastern situation would not serve the broad interests of the United States.

subfiles.title: Department-routed copy of Walter G. Hiltner's petition letter
subfiles.about: A routed copy repeats Hiltner's submission of Seattle church petitions against scrap-iron and war-material shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the text found on page 53 and bears Department routing and filing marks. Hiltner describes the Seattle dockside protest, opposition among labor, churches, and businesses, and the humanitarian case for stopping shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Green Lake United Presbyterian Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Green Lake United Presbyterian Church
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Church members appeal for legislation prohibiting scrap iron and munitions shipments to any aggressor nation.
subfiles.summary: The printed petition asks all branches of the federal government to hasten legislation banning scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor states. Two pages contain signatures and Seattle addresses from members of the Green Lake United Presbyterian Church and its congregation.

subfiles.title: Sea View Methodist Protestant Church petition
subfiles.from: Members of Sea View Methodist Protestant Church
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Sea View church members request legislation barring shipments of scrap iron and munitions to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: The petition uses language parallel to the Green Lake appeal and is signed by members of the Sea View Methodist Protestant Church in Seattle. It asks the executive and legislative branches to prohibit scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressor nations.

subfiles.title: Petition of Seattle residents
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: Seattle residents petition for legislation against scrap-iron and munitions shipments to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: This petition is framed for Seattle residents rather than a particular congregation. Much of the handwritten signature list is illegible in the OCR, but the request for federal legislation is clear.

subfiles.title: Sea View Methodist Protestant Church members and friends petition
subfiles.from: Members and friends of Sea View Methodist Protestant Church
subfiles.to: President, State Department, Senate, and House of Representatives
subfiles.about: A further Sea View petition asks for legislation prohibiting scrap-iron and munitions exports to aggressor nations.
subfiles.summary: The page repeats the appeal made by the other Seattle church petitions, now on behalf of Sea View members and friends. It contains an additional handwritten list of supporters and addresses.
